slides.say: Given: x plus four, in absolute value, is equal to three x. Which of the following gives all the possible values of x?

Now there's a letter on the right side too. This is the first time we meet it, and it changes one thing. We'll have to check every answer we get. [short pause] Two ways, two cases with a check, and then a shortcut.
at: a letter on the right side

slides.say: [short pause] Our first method. Two cases, as usual. Case one, x plus four is three x. Take x off both sides, four is two x, so x is two.
Case two, x plus four is minus three x. Add three x to both sides and take four off. Four x is minus four, so x is minus one.
Now the check. Why do we need it here? Because there's an x on both sides. When the other side is a plain number, you don't need to check. When it's a letter, you must.
x is two. Two plus four is six, in bars six. And three times two is six. It works.
x is minus one. Minus one plus four is three, in bars three. But three times minus one is minus three. Three isn't minus three, so minus one is fake.
Now careful, number three keeps the fake answer, and that's the trap. A lot of students stop right after the two cases. So only two, number one is our answer.
[pause] Our second method, a shortcut that starts from the right side. The bars are never negative, so the right side can't be negative. Three x is zero or positive, so x is zero or positive.
at: Three x is zero or positive

slides.say: And what does that mean for the bars? If x is zero or positive, x plus four is positive, so the bars do nothing. I can just drop them. x plus four is three x, so four is two x, and x is two.

So two is the only value. Numbers two and three have minus one in them, and x can't be negative here, so they're out. Number four says there's no such number, but two is one, so it's out too. Two only, number one.
So a letter on the right side? The right side must be zero or positive, and check every answer in the original equation. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
